title: Managing several levels of subordination
learning_objective: Keep subjects, clause boundaries and verb groups clear in a sentence with nested clauses.
summary: A subordinate clause can contain another subordinate clause.
explanation: A subordinate clause can contain another subordinate clause. Each clause has its own grammatical subject and verb group. Find the structure from the outside inward: identify what the main clause asserts, then which clause supplies the content, reason or condition. Several verbs at the end do not automatically belong to one group. If the nesting obscures the main point, divide the sentence into two sentences. Accuracy includes choosing a readable structure rather than maximizing sentence length.
rule: Identify each clause's subject and finite verb. Distinguish a nested clause from a single verb cluster. Split a sentence when the hierarchy becomes hard to follow.
example_dutch_1: Ik denk dat we moeten wachten totdat duidelijk is welke gegevens ontbreken.
example_english_1: I think we should wait until it is clear which data are missing.
example_dutch_2: Ze vroeg of ik wist waarom de vergadering was verplaatst.
example_english_2: She asked whether I knew why the meeting had been rescheduled.
common_mistake: Do not move all verbs into one undifferentiated final group.
notes: Extends B1 subordinate clauses with nested content and question clauses.

title: Placing known and new information in the middle field
learning_objective: Use object and adverb placement to distinguish familiar information from a new assertion.
summary: Within the Dutch middle field, order is influenced by definiteness, length and emphasis as well as grammatical role.
explanation: Within the Dutch middle field, order is influenced by definiteness, length and emphasis as well as grammatical role. A short, unstressed pronoun usually occurs early. A full noun phrase may occur later when it introduces new information or carries contrast. Time, manner and place are useful labels but not an inflexible ordering algorithm. Compare sentences in context and ask which part answers the current question. Preserve the finite-verb position and final verb group while adjusting the middle field.
rule: Place weak pronouns early. Give heavy or newly introduced material enough space. Use context and stress to interpret alternative orders.
example_dutch_1: Ik heb het gisteren aan de nieuwe projectleider uitgelegd.
example_english_1: I explained it to the new project leader yesterday.
example_dutch_2: We hebben gisteren een uitgebreid voorstel van de gemeente ontvangen.
example_english_2: Yesterday we received a detailed proposal from the municipality.
common_mistake: Do not reject every order that differs from a rigid time-manner-place list.
notes: Extends b1-long-sentence-bracket with information structure and object weight.

title: Using longer verb groups with replacement infinitives
learning_objective: Construct common subordinate perfect groups containing a modal and another infinitive.
summary: In a perfect construction with a modal and its dependent infinitive, the modal takes the replacement infinitive.
explanation: In a perfect construction with a modal and its dependent infinitive, the modal takes the replacement infinitive. In a subordinate clause, the finite auxiliary commonly comes before the two infinitives: dat zij heeft moeten vertrekken. This differs from the freer order of a simple auxiliary and participle. Separable particles and additional infinitives can create regional and stylistic variation; learn common Netherlands Dutch patterns before experimenting with alternatives. A long cluster is not a reason to add te after an ordinary modal.
rule: Use the replacement infinitive where the construction requires it. Prefer heeft moeten werken in a subordinate clause. Do not transfer two-verb participle variation to every larger group.
example_dutch_1: Ze legde uit dat ze onverwacht had moeten vertrekken.
example_english_1: She explained that she had had to leave unexpectedly.
example_dutch_2: Ik ben blij dat we het probleem hebben kunnen oplossen.
example_english_2: I am glad that we were able to solve the problem.
common_mistake: Avoid: dat we het probleem hebben gekund oplossen.
notes: Extends b1-perfect-modals and b1-subordinate-verb-groups.

title: Moving heavy information after the final verb group
learning_objective: Use a natural afterfield while keeping core sentence structure clear.
summary: A long prepositional phrase or subordinate clause can occur after the final verb group.
explanation: A long prepositional phrase or subordinate clause can occur after the final verb group. This afterfield can prevent a sentence bracket from becoming difficult to process. Not every constituent can be moved there equally freely: an ordinary unstressed object should not be treated as an afterthought by default. Extraposition is especially useful when a complement clause is long. Keep the relationship between the postponed material and its governing verb or noun clear.
rule: Use the afterfield for a heavy phrase or clause when natural. Keep weak pronouns in the middle field. Avoid placing essential short objects after the verb group mechanically.
example_dutch_1: We hebben lang gesproken over de gevolgen van het nieuwe beleid.
example_english_1: We talked at length about the consequences of the new policy.
example_dutch_2: Ik had niet verwacht dat de onderhandelingen zo lang zouden duren.
example_english_2: I had not expected the negotiations to last so long.
common_mistake: Do not confuse normal extraposition with the unrestricted English placement of objects after verbs.
notes: Extends B1 sentence brackets to a controlled afterfield.

title: Fronting an object to mark a contrast
learning_objective: Move an object or complement to the beginning without confusing it with the subject.
summary: The first position can contain an object or complement that is contrasted with another possibility.
explanation: The first position can contain an object or complement that is contrasted with another possibility. Main-clause verb-second order remains in force, so the subject follows the finite verb. Context and pronoun case help identify the grammatical roles. Fronting is useful for comparing alternatives or maintaining a topic across sentences; repeated unusual fronting can sound heavy. If the fronted phrase is resumed by a pronoun, that is a different spoken topic construction, not the same basic pattern.
rule: Identify the fronted element's role. Keep the finite verb second. Use contrastive fronting when the context gives a reason for it.
example_dutch_1: Die conclusie kan ik niet ondersteunen.
example_english_1: I cannot support that conclusion.
example_dutch_2: Over de planning zijn we het eens, maar over het budget nog niet.
example_english_2: We agree about the schedule, but not yet about the budget.
common_mistake: Do not assume the first noun phrase must be the subject.
notes: Adds deliberate contrastive focus beyond B1 fronted time clauses.

title: Highlighting a person, thing or reason with a cleft
learning_objective: Use het is ... die/dat and wat ... is to emphasize a selected element.
summary: A cleft divides a proposition into a highlighting clause and a clause that supplies the remaining information.
explanation: A cleft divides a proposition into a highlighting clause and a clause that supplies the remaining information. Het is Noor die ... highlights a person. Wat we nodig hebben, is ... highlights the answer to an open description. The relative element depends on the construction, so avoid copying English it is ... that word for word in every case. Clefts are useful for correction and emphasis but can make an otherwise simple paragraph unnecessarily elaborate.
rule: Use a cleft to identify the focused element. Keep the relative clause's verbs in subordinate order. Use wat when the opening clause has no explicit noun antecedent.
example_dutch_1: Het is de planning die ons de meeste problemen oplevert.
example_english_1: It is the schedule that causes us the most problems.
example_dutch_2: Wat we nu nodig hebben, is een duidelijke beslissing.
example_english_2: What we need now is a clear decision.
common_mistake: Avoid adding a cleft merely to make every sentence sound formal.
notes: Extends relative clauses into information packaging and corrective emphasis.

title: Distinguishing identifying information from extra information
learning_objective: Use context and punctuation to distinguish two functions of a relative clause.
summary: An identifying relative clause limits which people or things are meant.
explanation: An identifying relative clause limits which people or things are meant. A supplementary relative clause adds information about an already identified referent and is normally set off with commas. The distinction can change the claim: colleagues who work remotely may be only some colleagues, whereas a parenthetical clause can characterize the entire already identified group. Dutch does not adopt the English which-versus-that distinction as a universal rule; die and dat still depend on Dutch grammar.
rule: Ask whether the clause identifies a subset or adds a comment. Set supplementary information off with commas. Do not transfer an English punctuation rule mechanically.
example_dutch_1: De medewerkers die thuiswerken, krijgen een extra beeldscherm.
example_english_1: The employees who work from home receive an additional monitor.
example_dutch_2: Onze directeur, die meestal thuiswerkt, komt morgen naar kantoor.
example_english_2: Our director, who usually works from home, is coming to the office tomorrow.
common_mistake: Do not treat commas as purely decorative; they can affect the intended reference.
notes: Extends b1-embedded-relative-clauses with reference and punctuation.

title: Using wie and wat without a stated antecedent
learning_objective: Create a clause that means whoever or what without first naming a noun.
summary: A free relative clause has no separately stated noun antecedent.
explanation: A free relative clause has no separately stated noun antecedent. Wie refers to a person or people, while wat refers to a thing, action or idea. The entire clause can function as a subject or object. A main clause following an initial free relative still has its own structure. Wie can express a general condition, as in wie te laat komt, mist de uitleg. Distinguish this construction from an indirect question, even though the forms may look similar.
rule: Use wie for a person and wat for a thing or idea. Treat the complete free relative as one constituent. Identify its function in the main clause.
example_dutch_1: Wie zich op tijd aanmeldt, ontvangt een bevestiging.
example_english_1: Anyone who registers in time receives a confirmation.
example_dutch_2: Ik waardeer wat je voor het team hebt gedaan.
example_english_2: I appreciate what you have done for the team.
common_mistake: Do not add an unnecessary dat after wie or wat.
notes: Extends b1-relative-wat from stated antecedents to free relatives.

title: Expressing possession inside a relative clause
learning_objective: Choose a clear possessive relative construction for people and things.
summary: Possession can be expressed with a relative clause containing van wie or waarvan.
explanation: Possession can be expressed with a relative clause containing van wie or waarvan. In formal writing, wiens and wier also occur, but they are much less common in everyday speech and require care with their referents. A plain van wie construction is often more accessible. For a thing, waarvan ... het/de can express a part-whole relationship. Make the possessed noun and its article clear rather than omitting them to imitate English whose.
rule: Prefer clear van wie or waarvan constructions in ordinary use. Recognize wiens and wier in formal texts. Keep the possessed noun explicit.
example_dutch_1: Dat is de onderzoeker van wie het artikel gisteren verscheen.
example_english_1: That is the researcher whose article appeared yesterday.
example_dutch_2: We bezochten een gebouw waarvan het dak onlangs is vernieuwd.
example_english_2: We visited a building whose roof was recently replaced.
common_mistake: Do not use wie for an inanimate antecedent merely because English uses whose.
notes: Extends b1-relative-prepositions with possession; formal alternatives are for recognition and careful use.

title: Using a passive without a personal subject
learning_objective: Describe an activity with er when there is no direct object to become the subject.
summary: Some intransitive activities can be expressed in an impersonal passive.
explanation: Some intransitive activities can be expressed in an impersonal passive. Er often occupies the subject-related position, while the finite verb remains singular: er wordt gewerkt. The construction focuses on an activity taking place, not on an object being acted upon. It is common in announcements and descriptions. Not every intransitive verb permits this naturally; states and events without an acting participant often resist it. Do not invent a personal subject merely to match English.
rule: Use singular wordt or werd in an impersonal passive. Use the construction for suitable activities. Distinguish this er from quantitative or prepositional er.
example_dutch_1: Er wordt in deze ruimte niet gerookt.
example_english_1: There is no smoking in this room.
example_dutch_2: Tijdens de bijeenkomst werd uitvoerig over het voorstel gesproken.
example_english_2: The proposal was discussed at length during the meeting.
common_mistake: Avoid plural agreement with an object inside a prepositional phrase.
notes: Extends B1 personal passives to activities without a promoted direct object.

title: Combining passive meaning with modals and perfect infinitives
learning_objective: Use worden or zijn inside a modal construction while preserving the time relationship.
summary: A modal can govern a passive infinitive group: moet worden gecontroleerd expresses a required checking process.
explanation: A modal can govern a passive infinitive group: moet worden gecontroleerd expresses a required checking process. Moet zijn gecontroleerd normally means that the check must already be complete or that completion is inferred, depending on context. The lexical participle stays unchanged. Keep the distinction between obligation about a future process and a statement about a completed result. Adding more auxiliaries should make the timeline more precise, not simply make the sentence longer.
rule: Use modal plus worden plus participle for a passive process. Use zijn plus participle when completion is relevant. Interpret the modal in context.
example_dutch_1: Het formulier moet vóór vrijdag worden ingeleverd.
example_english_1: The form must be submitted before Friday.
example_dutch_2: De betaling moet inmiddels zijn verwerkt.
example_english_2: The payment must have been processed by now.
common_mistake: Do not treat worden and zijn as interchangeable after a modal.
notes: Extends B1 passive forms through modality and relative completion.

title: Distinguishing a passive event from an adjectival state
learning_objective: Use context and construction to distinguish an action from its resulting state.
summary: A participle can be part of a verbal passive or describe a state like an adjective.
explanation: A participle can be part of a verbal passive or describe a state like an adjective. De deur wordt gesloten presents a process; de deur is gesloten can report a completed action or describe its result. A clear adjective such as dicht removes some of that ambiguity. Event-related adverbs and an actor phrase can favour a verbal reading, while a description of an enduring condition can favour an adjectival reading. The boundary is not always sharp.
rule: Use worden to foreground a process. Use an ordinary adjective when you specifically mean a state and one is available. Read participles in context.
example_dutch_1: De winkel wordt om zes uur gesloten.
example_english_1: The shop is closed at six o'clock.
example_dutch_2: De winkel is vandaag dicht wegens onderhoud.
example_english_2: The shop is closed today for maintenance.
common_mistake: Do not label every occurrence of zijn plus participle as exactly the same tense or meaning.
notes: Extends b1-passive-perfect with the verbal-adjectival distinction.

title: Understanding krijgen with a participle
learning_objective: Recognize constructions that make the recipient the subject.
summary: Krijgen with a participle can foreground a recipient rather than the direct object of an active clause.
explanation: Krijgen with a participle can foreground a recipient rather than the direct object of an active clause. In zij krijgt de prijs uitgereikt, zij receives something that someone presents. This pattern occurs with verbs involving transfer, communication or assignment, but it is not a universal substitute for worden. A direct object may remain in the sentence. Learn natural combinations such as iets aangeboden, uitgelegd or toegewezen krijgen.
rule: Interpret the subject as the recipient. Retain the thing transferred or explained as an object. Do not use krijgen with every passive verb.
example_dutch_1: De winnaar kreeg de prijs persoonlijk uitgereikt.
example_english_1: The winner was presented with the prize in person.
example_dutch_2: We krijgen de resultaten volgende week toegestuurd.
example_english_2: The results will be sent to us next week.
common_mistake: Avoid assuming that the remaining noun phrase must become the grammatical subject.
notes: Adds a recipient-oriented construction beyond the B1 worden passive.

title: Controlling tense and viewpoint in longer reports
learning_objective: Keep time, certainty and attribution distinct in a report of several statements.
summary: Dutch reported speech allows a choice of tense according to the intended time and viewpoint.
explanation: Dutch reported speech allows a choice of tense according to the intended time and viewpoint. A past reporting verb does not force all following verbs into the past. Preserve a present tense for continuing facts when appropriate; use a past or pluperfect form to locate an event relative to the original statement. Make it clear which claims belong to the source and which belong to the current writer. Reintroduce the source when a long passage could blur that boundary.
rule: Anchor each tense to a reference point. Keep source attribution clear. Use time expressions to prevent an accidental shift from the source's viewpoint to the writer's.
example_dutch_1: De woordvoerder zei dat de regeling nog steeds geldt.
example_english_1: The spokesperson said that the scheme is still in force.
example_dutch_2: Volgens de manager had het team de fout al hersteld voordat de klacht binnenkwam.
example_english_2: According to the manager, the team had already corrected the error before the complaint arrived.
common_mistake: Do not interpret every change of tense as a mandatory mechanical backshift.
notes: Extends b1-reported-speech to sustained reporting and multiple time relationships.

title: Reporting uncertain or unconfirmed information
learning_objective: Distinguish a reported claim from the speaker's own confirmed assertion.
summary: Zou can signal information attributed to another source without presenting it as independently confirmed.
explanation: Zou can signal information attributed to another source without presenting it as independently confirmed. This reported or evidential use differs from a future-in-the-past and from a condition. Volgens plus a source, naar verluidt and an explicit reporting clause help establish the intended reading. Avoid using a distancing form to imply doubt that the context does not justify. For a confirmed fact, an ordinary assertion with a source reference may be clearer.
rule: Distinguish reported zou from hypothetical zou. Identify the source where possible. Use register-appropriate expressions of uncertainty.
example_dutch_1: Volgens de krant zou het bedrijf volgend jaar uitbreiden.
example_english_1: According to the newspaper, the company is reportedly planning to expand next year.
example_dutch_2: De afspraak zou zijn verplaatst, maar ik heb nog geen bevestiging ontvangen.
example_english_2: The appointment has reportedly been rescheduled, but I have not received confirmation yet.
common_mistake: Do not translate every zou with a single English would regardless of its function.
notes: Extends b1-future-in-the-past and reported speech with evidential distance.

title: Using moeten, zullen and kunnen for deductions
learning_objective: Distinguish logical inference from obligation, prediction and ability.
summary: Modal verbs can express a judgment about how likely something is.
explanation: Modal verbs can express a judgment about how likely something is. Moeten can present a strong deduction, zullen an expectation or assumption, and kunnen a possibility. The same forms also have practical meanings such as obligation and ability. A perfect infinitive places the inferred event earlier: hij moet vertrokken zijn. Context and adverbs distinguish the readings. Negation also matters: kan niet zijn often rules out a possibility rather than describing an inability.
rule: Identify whether the modal concerns facts or permitted actions. Use a perfect infinitive for an earlier event. Do not assign one fixed meaning to each modal.
example_dutch_1: Het licht is uit; iedereen zal wel naar huis zijn.
example_english_1: The lights are off; everyone has probably gone home.
example_dutch_2: Ze moet de verkeerde trein hebben genomen.
example_english_2: She must have taken the wrong train.
common_mistake: Do not interpret moet in the second sentence as an instruction issued in the past.
notes: Extends B1 modals with epistemic meaning and earlier-event deductions.

title: Distinguishing no obligation, prohibition and impossibility
learning_objective: Use negation with modal verbs to express the intended scope.
summary: Niet hoeven means that an action is unnecessary, while niet mogen normally means that it is not allowed.
explanation: Niet hoeven means that an action is unnecessary, while niet mogen normally means that it is not allowed. Niet moeten can express advice against an action, a prohibition-like instruction or a contrast in what is required, depending on context. Kunnen with negation can express inability or rule out a possibility. Use an unambiguous alternative when practical consequences depend on the distinction. Hoeven takes te with an infinitive in the usual negative or restrictive construction.
rule: Use niet hoeven te for absence of necessity. Use niet mogen for prohibition. Check whether negation applies to the obligation or to the action.
example_dutch_1: Je hoeft het formulier niet opnieuw in te vullen.
example_english_1: You do not need to fill in the form again.
example_dutch_2: Je mag deze gegevens niet zonder toestemming delen.
example_english_2: You may not share these data without permission.
common_mistake: Do not translate don't have to with mag niet.
notes: Extends earlier modal patterns through explicit scope contrasts.

title: Using lijken, blijken and schijnen with te
learning_objective: Express appearance, discovery and reported impression through a te-infinitive.
summary: Lijken te presents an appearance or impression.
explanation: Lijken te presents an appearance or impression. Blijken te presents something that becomes evident. Schijnen te can suggest an impression or information heard indirectly. The grammatical subject belongs meaningfully to the infinitive action or state: de maatregel blijkt te werken. A perfect infinitive, such as te hebben gewerkt, refers to an earlier situation. These constructions help separate observed facts from impressions without requiring an impersonal English it construction.
rule: Use te before the infinitive. Choose the verb according to the evidence. Use a perfect infinitive for an earlier situation.
example_dutch_1: De nieuwe aanpak blijkt goed te werken.
example_english_1: The new approach turns out to work well.
example_dutch_2: Hij schijnt de uitnodiging niet te hebben ontvangen.
example_english_2: Apparently, he did not receive the invitation.
common_mistake: Do not treat lijken, blijken and schijnen as interchangeable synonyms.
notes: Extends B1 infinitive complements into evidential meaning.

title: Recognizing meaning shifts in te constructions
learning_objective: Interpret verbs such as weten, dreigen and beloven when they govern an infinitive.
summary: Some verbs develop a construction-specific meaning with te.
explanation: Some verbs develop a construction-specific meaning with te. Weten te often means manage to, while dreigen te can mean that an undesirable event is about to happen, without a person issuing a threat. Beloven te can express a promising prospect as well as an actual promise, depending on its subject. Interpret the whole construction. An inanimate subject may be a useful clue that the verb is not describing a deliberate speech act.
rule: Read the governing verb together with its infinitive. Distinguish literal speech acts from event-related meanings. Check the subject and context.
example_dutch_1: Het team wist de achterstand in te halen.
example_english_1: The team managed to make up the deficit.
example_dutch_2: De onderhandelingen dreigen vast te lopen.
example_english_2: The negotiations are threatening to break down.
common_mistake: Do not translate weten te as know to in every sentence.
notes: Adds constructional meanings beyond B1 subject-controlled infinitives.

title: Reporting perceived actions in the perfect
learning_objective: Combine perception verbs with the replacement infinitive and preserve the performer.
summary: In a perfect construction such as ik heb haar zien vertrekken, zien is a replacement infinitive and haar is the performer of vertrekken.
explanation: In a perfect construction such as ik heb haar zien vertrekken, zien is a replacement infinitive and haar is the performer of vertrekken. The final action is presented as something perceived. Compare this with ik heb gezien dat zij vertrok, which uses an ordinary participle and a finite content clause. The two patterns can differ in perspective and emphasis. Keep te out of the ordinary object-plus-perception-infinitive pattern.
rule: Use heb plus object plus zien/horen plus infinitive. Use gezien/gehoord in an appropriate finite-clause alternative. Identify who performs the perceived action.
example_dutch_1: Ik heb haar het gebouw zien verlaten.
example_english_1: I saw her leave the building.
example_dutch_2: We hebben gehoord dat de vergadering niet doorgaat.
example_english_2: We heard that the meeting is not going ahead.
common_mistake: Avoid: Ik heb haar gezien te vertrekken.
notes: Extends b1-laten-and-perception and b1-perfect-modals.

title: Expressing possibility and necessity with te constructions
learning_objective: Understand expressions such as te bereiken and er valt te ... without inventing an actor.
summary: Zijn plus a te-infinitive can describe something as possible or suitable for an action: de tekst is goed te lezen.
explanation: Zijn plus a te-infinitive can describe something as possible or suitable for an action: de tekst is goed te lezen. A modal or adjective in context may add necessity or evaluation. Er valt te ... often presents a possibility or something available to be done. The grammatical subject of zijn is commonly the thing affected by the infinitive, not its performer. These expressions differ from the ordinary active te-clause after proberen.
rule: Distinguish the affected thing from the performer. Interpret possibility or necessity from context. Recognize natural combinations rather than applying the construction to every verb.
example_dutch_1: De locatie is goed met het openbaar vervoer te bereiken.
example_english_1: The venue is easy to reach by public transport.
example_dutch_2: Er valt nog veel te verbeteren aan deze werkwijze.
example_english_2: There is still a lot that can be improved about this way of working.
common_mistake: Do not interpret de locatie as the performer of bereiken.
notes: Adds passive-like possibility constructions to the B1 infinitive system.

title: Imagining a different outcome in the past
learning_objective: Use a pluperfect condition and a perfect result for an unreal past alternative.
summary: A past counterfactual describes a situation that did not happen, or is presented as contrary to the known past.
explanation: A past counterfactual describes a situation that did not happen, or is presented as contrary to the known past. The condition commonly uses had or was plus a participle. The result may use zou plus a perfect infinitive, or a pluperfect form in a compact alternative. Choose hebben or zijn according to the construction and intended meaning. A counterfactual differs from an ordinary earlier-past explanation because the alternative is imagined.
rule: Use als plus pluperfect for the unreal past condition. Use zou hebben/zijn plus participle for the result when appropriate. Keep the actual and imagined timelines distinct.
example_dutch_1: Als ik de waarschuwing had gelezen, zou ik een andere route hebben gekozen.
example_english_1: If I had read the warning, I would have chosen a different route.
example_dutch_2: Als we eerder waren vertrokken, hadden we de trein gehaald.
example_english_2: If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train.
common_mistake: Do not use a present infinitive result when you specifically mean a completed past alternative.
notes: Extends b1-hypothetical-present and b1-pluperfect-sequencing.

title: Linking a past condition to a present consequence
learning_objective: Express an unreal relationship whose condition and result refer to different times.
summary: The condition and result of a hypothetical sentence do not have to refer to the same time.
explanation: The condition and result of a hypothetical sentence do not have to refer to the same time. A different past decision can imply a different present situation. A lasting present characteristic can also explain an imagined past outcome. Choose each tense according to its own reference point rather than forcing both clauses into a memorized pair. Add nu or toen when needed to make the intended times clear.
rule: Anchor the condition and result separately. Use explicit time expressions when helpful. Preserve the distinction between a present state and a completed event.
example_dutch_1: Als ik die opleiding had gevolgd, zou ik nu meer mogelijkheden hebben.
example_english_1: If I had taken that course, I would have more opportunities now.
example_dutch_2: Als hij beter Frans sprak, had hij het gesprek gisteren zelf kunnen voeren.
example_english_2: If he spoke French better, he could have conducted the conversation himself yesterday.
common_mistake: Do not assume both clauses must refer to the past because one contains had.
notes: Extends past counterfactuals with independently chosen time references.

title: Setting conditions with mits and tenzij
learning_objective: Distinguish provided that from unless without reversing the condition.
summary: Mits introduces a positive requirement that must be satisfied.
explanation: Mits introduces a positive requirement that must be satisfied. Tenzij introduces an exception that prevents the main statement from applying. Both take subordinate word order. Because tenzij already contributes an except-if relationship, adding a negative can reverse the intended meaning. When a condition has practical importance, paraphrase it mentally with als or behalve als to check it. These connectors are useful in careful discussion and written agreements without requiring specialist legal language.
rule: Use mits for a required positive condition. Use tenzij for an exception. Check the scope of any additional negation.
example_dutch_1: Je kunt deelnemen, mits je je vooraf aanmeldt.
example_english_1: You can take part provided that you register in advance.
example_dutch_2: We gaan fietsen, tenzij het hard regent.
example_english_2: We will go cycling unless it rains heavily.
common_mistake: Do not use mits when you mean unless.
notes: Extends B1 hypothetical language with explicit limits and exceptions.

title: Separating an acknowledged fact from a hypothetical obstacle
learning_objective: Distinguish hoewel, ook al and zelfs als in more nuanced arguments.
summary: Hoewel usually concedes a fact.
explanation: Hoewel usually concedes a fact. Zelfs als can present a hypothetical situation that would not change the conclusion. Ook al can express a factual concession or an imagined obstacle depending on context, and it uses inversion within its own clause. An initial concessive clause is followed by the normal structure of the main clause. Use these differences to avoid presenting an uncertain claim as an established fact.
rule: Use zelfs als for even if when the condition is hypothetical. Use hoewel for a conceded fact. Keep the special inversion after ook al.
example_dutch_1: Zelfs als iedereen akkoord gaat, moeten we het plan nog toetsen.
example_english_1: Even if everyone agrees, we still need to assess the plan.
example_dutch_2: Ook al zou het goedkoper zijn, ik kies niet voor die oplossing.
example_english_2: Even if it were cheaper, I would not choose that solution.
common_mistake: Do not make hoewel imply a hypothetical condition when the intended meaning is even if.
notes: Extends b1-concession-hoewel-ook-al into argumentation and hypothetical scope.

title: Relating two changing quantities with hoe ... hoe
learning_objective: Express a systematic relationship between two degrees or quantities.
summary: Hoe ...
explanation: Hoe ... hoe links two changing degrees, as in the more ..., the less .... Both parts contain a comparative expression or an equivalent quantity expression. The second part commonly has an ordering pattern such as hoe langer ik wacht, hoe onrustiger ik word. Des te is an alternative in the second part and can give the expression a more formal tone. This is different from a direct question beginning with hoe.
rule: Use a comparative or quantity in each part. Keep each clause's internal structure clear. Recognize des te as an alternative, not an obligatory extra marker.
example_dutch_1: Hoe beter we ons voorbereiden, hoe soepeler het gesprek verloopt.
example_english_1: The better we prepare, the more smoothly the conversation goes.
example_dutch_2: Hoe langer ik erover nadenk, des te minder begrijp ik het besluit.
example_english_2: The longer I think about it, the less I understand the decision.
common_mistake: Do not interpret the first hoe as a direct question requiring ordinary question inversion.
notes: Extends B1 degree comparisons to proportional relationships.

title: Using particles to guide the listener's interpretation
learning_objective: Recognize how wel, toch, eens and maar soften, reinforce or frame an utterance.
summary: Small particles often change the interpersonal meaning without changing the basic proposition.
explanation: Small particles often change the interpersonal meaning without changing the basic proposition. Maar can make an invitation more permissive, eens can make a request less abrupt, and toch can invoke a shared expectation. Wel may reassure or contradict a negative assumption. Their effect depends on stress, intonation and context, so one-word English equivalents are unreliable. In formal writing, use them selectively when the intended tone remains clear.
rule: Interpret a particle in its full utterance. Distinguish unstressed particles from stressed contrasts. Avoid stacking particles without understanding the effect.
example_dutch_1: Kom maar binnen; we hebben nog genoeg tijd.
example_english_1: Come on in; we still have plenty of time.
example_dutch_2: Dat komt wel goed, denk ik.
example_english_2: I think it will work out all right.
common_mistake: Do not translate maar as but when it is functioning as a permissive particle.
notes: Extends B1 contrast and wishes with pragmatic meaning in modern Netherlands Dutch.

title: Keeping pronoun reference clear across sentences
learning_objective: Maintain clear references when several people, objects or ideas are being discussed.
summary: A pronoun should have a recoverable referent.
explanation: A pronoun should have a recoverable referent. When two recent noun phrases could both match it, repeating a noun or using a more explicit phrase is often better than adding another pronoun. Dit and dat can point to a whole statement, while hij, zij and het usually maintain a more specific referent. A grammatical agreement match alone does not guarantee that the reader will choose the intended antecedent. Check reference across paragraph boundaries as well as within a sentence.
rule: Repeat a noun when a pronoun would be ambiguous. Distinguish reference to a noun from reference to a whole proposition. Track changes of speaker in reported passages.
example_dutch_1: Noor besprak het voorstel met Sara. Daarna stuurde Noor een samenvatting.
example_english_1: Noor discussed the proposal with Sara. Noor then sent a summary.
example_dutch_2: De levering is opnieuw vertraagd. Dat maakt onze planning onzeker.
example_english_2: The delivery has been delayed again. That makes our schedule uncertain.
common_mistake: Do not assume the nearest grammatically matching noun is always the intended referent.
notes: Extends B1 pronouns and reported information to sustained discourse.

title: Recognizing several functions served by er
learning_objective: Analyze sentences in which er combines with quantity, location or a preposition.
summary: Er can have a locative, quantitative, prepositional or presentational function.
explanation: Er can have a locative, quantitative, prepositional or presentational function. In some sentences one unstressed er serves more than one recoverable role; repeating er for every function is often unnatural. In ik heb er drie van meegenomen, the quantity and the van relationship work together. Presentational and quantitative er can also occur separately in one sentence, as in er staan er nog twee; two occurrences are not automatically wrong. Diagnose each function by restoring the fuller noun or phrase, then choose a natural compact sentence. When the reference would be unclear, repeat the noun instead.
rule: Identify the omitted noun or phrase for each function. Do not mechanically multiply er. Keep the required prepositional element and quantity.
example_dutch_1: Ik heb er gisteren drie van meegenomen.
example_english_1: I took three of them with me yesterday.
example_dutch_2: Er staan er nog twee in de gang.
example_english_2: There are still two of them in the corridor.
common_mistake: The two occurrences in the second example have different roles; do not assume all repetition is forbidden.
notes: Extends b1-er-prepositional and b1-er-quantity-in-longer-clauses through combined functions.

title: Separating er, daar and waar from their prepositional elements
learning_objective: Use separated pronominal adverbs while keeping their reference and attachment clear.
summary: Ermee and daarmee can be split when other material intervenes: daar ben ik het niet mee eens.
explanation: Ermee and daarmee can be split when other material intervenes: daar ben ik het niet mee eens. Waar compounds in questions and relatives can also be separated in ordinary usage. The prepositional element still belongs to the original combination. Distinguish it from an identical-looking separable verb particle. Stress often favours daar or hier over weak er. For people, a preposition plus a personal or relative pronoun is usually the clearer choice.
rule: Keep track of the governing expression and its preposition. Distinguish a prepositional adverb from a verb particle. Use daar or hier for contrastive reference when appropriate.
example_dutch_1: Daar heb ik tijdens het overleg al op gewezen.
example_english_1: I already pointed that out during the meeting.
example_dutch_2: Waar hebben jullie zo lang over gesproken?
example_english_2: What did you talk about for so long?
common_mistake: Do not drop op from wijzen op when the object is replaced by daar.
notes: Extends B1 er and relative-preposition constructions with distance and emphasis.

title: Using participles to describe a noun compactly
learning_objective: Turn suitable event information into an accurate participial modifier.
summary: A participle before a noun can express a resulting condition or a completed action affecting that noun.
explanation: A participle before a noun can express a resulting condition or a completed action affecting that noun. It takes the adjective ending required by the noun phrase, as in de onlangs gerenoveerde woning. Present participles can describe an ongoing characteristic, but Dutch uses them more selectively than English -ing modifiers. Keep any accompanying adverb close to the participle. Do not use a participle that assigns the action to the wrong participant.
rule: Apply adjective inflection to an attributive participle. Check whether the noun performs or undergoes the action. Prefer an ordinary relative clause if the compact form is unclear.
example_dutch_1: De onlangs gepubliceerde resultaten bevestigen onze verwachting.
example_english_1: The recently published results confirm our expectation.
example_dutch_2: We zoeken een passende oplossing voor beide partijen.
example_english_2: We are looking for a suitable solution for both parties.
common_mistake: Do not leave an attributive participle uninflected merely because it is derived from a verb.
notes: Extends A2 adjective endings and B1 passive meaning into compact noun phrases.

title: Using compact introductory phrases without a dangling subject
learning_objective: Condense a suitable adverbial clause while keeping its understood subject correct.
summary: A compact introductory phrase such as eenmaal aangekomen can replace a fuller time clause when its understood subject matches the main-clause subject.
explanation: A compact introductory phrase such as eenmaal aangekomen can replace a fuller time clause when its understood subject matches the main-clause subject. A mismatch creates a dangling construction: a report cannot have arrived at a station simply because its writer did. These structures are common in written narrative and concise explanation. They are not necessary in every formal sentence; a full clause is often clearer when there is more than one possible performer.
rule: Make the understood subject match the main-clause subject. Use a full subordinate clause when the actors differ. Avoid compressing away an essential time relationship.
example_dutch_1: Eenmaal aangekomen op het station, zochten we het juiste perron.
example_english_1: Once we had arrived at the station, we looked for the right platform.
example_dutch_2: Na de gegevens te hebben gecontroleerd, verstuurde zij het rapport.
example_english_2: After checking the data, she sent the report.
common_mistake: Avoid: Aangekomen op het station, vertrok de trein when the intended arrival concerns the passengers.
notes: Extends B1 infinitive clauses and B2 participial modifiers to compact adverbial structures.

title: Choosing between an action clause and a nominalisation
learning_objective: Use an infinitive as a noun without making the sentence unnecessarily abstract.
summary: A nominalised infinitive normally takes het and can name an activity as a topic: het verwerken van de gegevens.
explanation: A nominalised infinitive normally takes het and can name an activity as a topic: het verwerken van de gegevens. Objects may be introduced by van in a noun-like structure. This can help discuss a process, but several nominalisations in a row can conceal who is responsible for an action. An active clause with an explicit subject is often clearer. Choose the structure according to the purpose and audience rather than equating abstraction with quality.
rule: Use het with a nominalised infinitive. Keep complements and agency clear. Replace excessive nominalisation with a finite clause when useful.
example_dutch_1: Het controleren van de gegevens kost meer tijd dan verwacht.
example_english_1: Checking the data takes more time than expected.
example_dutch_2: We controleren de gegevens voordat we het rapport publiceren.
example_english_2: We check the data before we publish the report.
common_mistake: Do not assume that a longer chain of abstract nouns is automatically more professional.
notes: Adds deliberate register choices beyond B1 clause linking.

title: Choosing an appropriate degree of impersonality
learning_objective: Choose between we, men, an active actor and a passive construction.
summary: Formal Dutch can use a named actor, we, men or a passive construction.
explanation: Formal Dutch can use a named actor, we, men or a passive construction. Each choice distributes responsibility and emphasis differently. Men refers generally to people but can sound distant when the actual actor is known. A passive is useful when the procedure matters more than the actor, but it can also obscure responsibility. Informal spoken topic constructions should not be copied mechanically into a carefully structured report. Prefer a clear, audience-appropriate sentence.
rule: Choose the actor or lack of actor deliberately. Use men with singular agreement. Do not use a passive solely to avoid saying who made a decision.
example_dutch_1: De commissie beoordeelt de aanvragen op vaste criteria.
example_english_1: The committee assesses applications against fixed criteria.
example_dutch_2: In dit rapport wordt onderscheid gemaakt tussen kosten en opbrengsten.
example_english_2: This report distinguishes between costs and revenue.
common_mistake: Avoid using men as a plural subject because it refers to several people.
notes: Integrates B1 passives with formal-versus-informal choices.

title: Omitting repeated material without breaking a parallel structure
learning_objective: Use coordinated clauses and ellipsis while preserving clear grammatical roles.
summary: Dutch can omit repeated material when the remaining parts form a clear parallel structure.
explanation: Dutch can omit repeated material when the remaining parts form a clear parallel structure. In Noor schrijft het verslag en Sam de samenvatting, the second clause omits schrijft. The omission must leave an understandable relationship; shared words cannot always be reused when they serve incompatible grammatical roles or require different forms. Check agreement and the complements required by each verb. In a dense paragraph, repeating a verb can be clearer than an ambitious ellipsis.
rule: Keep coordinated structures parallel. Omit only recoverable material. Check the agreement and complements of each clause separately.
example_dutch_1: Noor schrijft het verslag en Sam de samenvatting.
example_english_1: Noor writes the report and Sam the summary.
example_dutch_2: We hebben het voorstel besproken, aangepast en uiteindelijk goedgekeurd.
example_english_2: We discussed, revised and ultimately approved the proposal.
common_mistake: Do not coordinate phrases that need incompatible prepositions as though one preposition could serve both.
notes: Extends A1/A2 coordination to controlled omission and parallelism.

title: Linking claims, evidence and limitations clearly
learning_objective: Build a nuanced argument with explicit relationships and appropriately limited claims.
summary: A developed argument distinguishes a claim, supporting evidence, a concession and a conclusion.
explanation: A developed argument distinguishes a claim, supporting evidence, a concession and a conclusion. Linking expressions such as enerzijds ... anderzijds, bovendien and desondanks help only when they match the actual relationship. Modal expressions and phrases such as voor zover ik weet can limit a claim's strength. They do not substitute for evidence. Keep main-clause inversion after fronted linking adverbs and subordinate order after expressions introducing a subordinate clause.
rule: State the relationship between ideas explicitly. Balance paired connectors. Use a qualification only when it reflects the intended certainty or scope.
example_dutch_1: Enerzijds bespaart de maatregel geld; anderzijds vraagt hij veel extra werk.
example_english_1: On the one hand, the measure saves money; on the other hand, it requires a lot of extra work.
example_dutch_2: Voor zover ik kan beoordelen, wegen de voordelen op tegen de nadelen.
example_english_2: As far as I can judge, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.
common_mistake: Do not use a strong conclusion connector when the preceding sentence merely supplies an unrelated detail.
notes: Integrates B1 cohesion with B2 qualification, scope and balanced argumentation.
